questions.q: What is the childhood promise the speaker makes to her great-grandmother in the first section of the poem?
questions.a: The speaker promises: "When I grow old, / And very very rich / I shall rebuild the fallen walls / And make new this ancient house." A wrong answer (e.g., "she promises to visit often" or "she promises to pray for the house") reveals the student is confusing the speaker's vow with the great-grandmother's stories — they haven't distinguished between the two voices in the dialogue.

questions.q: In your own words, explain why the great-grandmother's "feasts were monotonous / For the only dish was always God."
questions.a: The line means the great-grandmother's spiritual devotion was total and exclusive — her life was sustained entirely by faith ("Fed on God for years"), leaving no room for worldly pleasures or variety. A wrong answer that focuses only on literal food ("she ate the same thing every day") shows the student misses the metaphor: "feasts" and "dish" represent spiritual sustenance, not meals. This is a comprehension error rooted in reading metaphor literally.

questions.q: Apply the concept of "thematic anchor" to the image of the elephant ride. How does this single memory support the primary theme of aristocratic loss?
questions.a: Step 1: Locate the elephant ride in stanza 3 — "she rode her elephant / When she was ten or eleven / Every Monday without fail / To the Siva shrine." Step 2: Identify what it represents: royal privilege, ritualised tradition, feminine grace ("sandal for her breasts," "perfumes and oils"). Step 3: Connect to theme — this memory contrasts sharply with the speaker's later admission: "to grow rich / Was a difficult feat." The elephant ride embodies the lost world the speaker can neither reclaim nor rebuild. Step 4: Note the irony — the great-grandmother's widowhood ("died of fever, in her arms / ... lovely short year") makes the ride a memory of lost power, not current status. A wrong answer that merely describes the ride ("she went to temple on an elephant") fails to link the image to the theme of irrecoverable heritage.

questions.q: Analyse the shift in the meaning of "blood" across the poem. How does this semantic evolution structure the primary theme?
questions.a: The word "blood" appears in three distinct registers: (1) Stanza 3: "oldest blood in the world / A blood thin and clear and fine" — aristocratic pride, purity, lineage. (2) Stanza 3 contrast: "veins of the always poor ... blood thick as gruel / And muddy as a ditch" — class prejudice disguised as biological fact. (3) Final stanza: "So thin, so clear, so fine / The oldest blood in the world / That remembers as it flows / All the gems and all the gold" — defensive reclamation, the blood becomes a witness that absolves the speaker. The theme is structured by this shift: from pride to prejudice to self-justification. A wrong answer that treats "blood" as a static symbol ("it means family") misses the poem's central tension — the speaker uses ancestry to excuse abandonment.

questions.q: Evaluate the speaker's final plea: "Call me callous / Call me selfish / But do not blame my blood." Is this a genuine moral defence or a rhetorical evasion? Justify with evidence.
questions.a: It is a rhetorical evasion. Evidence: (1) The speaker admits "I had learnt by then / Most lessons of defeat" — she chooses not to act, not inability. (2) "I have plucked your soul / Like a pip from a fruit / And have flung it into your pyre" — violent imagery shows active severance, not passive circumstance. (3) The blood "remembers as it flows / All the gems and all the gold" — the ancestry recalls luxury, not duty. The defence collapses because the blood remembers privilege but forgets responsibility. A wrong answer that accepts the plea at face value ("she's right, it's not her fault") fails to interrogate the speaker's unreliable narration — a key skill for Class 12 analysis.

questions.q: Create a four-line stanza that could serve as a "missing stanza" between the great-grandmother's death and the speaker's departure, capturing the moment the promise dies. Use the poem's imagery and tone.
questions.a: A strong answer will: (1) Use the house imagery (cracked walls, rats, moon), (2) Show the speaker's internal conflict (guilt vs practicality), (3) Echo the poem's free verse rhythm, (4) End on an image of departure or silence. Example: "The mortgage papers lay unsigned / The contractor never came / The moon watched through cracked windows / As I folded the promise into my suitcase." A weak answer that rhymes forcedly or uses generic sadness ("I felt so sad and cried") reveals the student hasn't internalised the poem's specific visual vocabulary or its restrained, image-driven tone.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The primary theme of a poem is its central, unifying idea — the core insight about human experience that the poet ______ through imagery, tone, structure, and language.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you're standing in front of your own ______ home, watching it crumble — you promised to fix it, but life got in the way.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can identify the primary theme of "Blood," trace its development across three distinct phases of the poem (childhood promise, adult failure, final confession), and explain how specific images (the house, the blood, the elephant ride) function as thematic anchors — all while using textual evidence in a structured PEEL.
